Data Resource Profile: A Florida-scale simulated dataset for developing and benchmarking record-linkage software for cancer data systems

Authors
Affiliations

Abraham D. Flaxman

University of Washington

Anders Alexandersson

University of Miami Miller School of Medicine

Abstract

Introduction … Methods … Results … Conclusion …

Keywords

record linkage, entity resolution, simulated data, cancer registry, benchmark dataset, reproducibility, pseudopeople

Key Features

  • What is unique: a large, fully simulated, multi-file dataset for linking individual people, with cross-file ground truth (every record carries a simulant_id, so missed-match and false-match rates of any method can be computed exactly rather than estimated), designed to capture the record matching challenges faced by a Florida-scale cancer data system.

  • Why created: linkage software for cancer registries must be developed and tested on names, dates of birth, addresses and SSNs, which are exactly the identifiers that confidentiality rules prevent registries from releasing.

  • Details: a simulated Florida drawn from the 50,518,675 simulated people recorded as residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 censuses, including a simulated registry of 5,000,002 records whose age and sex distribution is that of the cases reported by the Florida Cancer Data System, and researcher finder files of 500,000 and 100,001 records drawn from residents in 2040.

  • Data linkage: the larger finder file includes 100,000 people who are also in the registry and the smaller finder file includes 20,000. There is no overlap between the finder files.

  • Main categories of data: simulated person-level identifiers including name, date of birth, sex, street-address fields, SSN, race/ethnicity, and a diagnosis date on each registry record, carrying realistic synthetic noise (typos, nicknames, month/day swaps, blanks, duplications).

  • Access: direct download under a permissive licence with a DOI.

3 Results

We describe the released files first (Section 3.1), then the people in them (Section 3.2), the errors in their fields (Section 3.3) and how hard those errors make the files to link with exact rules (Section 3.4); every value below is computed from the released files or the build’s own summaries, and how the files were built is left to Section 2.

3.1 Structure, contents, and where the data are held

This data resource is a zip archive containing three comma-separated files, deposited on Zenodo under a DOI that will be minted before publication. The high-level characteristics of the files are described in Table 1: a simulated registry of 5,000,000 people and two finder files of 500,000 and 100,000 people. All three are drawn from Florida residents in the simulated 2020, 2030 or 2040 census, a pool of 50,518,675 distinct simulated people, counted once each across the three censuses, which span twenty years, and including people who died or left the state between them.

Every row of each file carries a simulant_id, the identifier of the simulated person it describes; the same identifier in two files means the same person, and this is the ground truth against which any other linkage of the files can be scored. The files also contain the fields that record linkage typically relies on: first name, middle initial, last name, date of birth, sex, race/ethnicity, street number, street name, unit number, city, state, ZIP code and social security number (SSN). Registry rows also carry a diagnosis date, which we placed on a day within the year of the census the record was drawn from, so that diagnoses fall in 2020, 2030 or 2040 only (Section 2; the consequences are weighed in Section 4). Addresses carry real Florida cities and ZIP codes but simulated street addresses that are not real street locations. The registry has 5,000,002 rows for its 5,000,000 people, and the finder files have 500,000 and 100,001 rows for 500,000 and 100,000 people; the few people with two rows are duplicated records, two differently transcribed rows for one person (Section 2).

The larger finder file shares 100,000 people with the registry, 20% of its records, and the smaller shares 20,000, the same 20% share; the two finder files share no people with each other. The 20% overlap was chosen to mirror the finder files FCDS receives (Section 2). A registry row and a finder row that carry the same identifier are a “true pair”, the unit on which every linkage result below is scored; the larger finder file holds 100,000 true pairs and the smaller 20,000, and every other pairing of a registry row with a finder row is a true non-match. Every finder record is drawn from the 2040 census, and so is the registry record of every person who appears in a finder file; people last seen in 2020 or 2030 appear in the registry alone (Section 4).

The archive also includes a manifest of MD5 and SHA-256 digests (Table 1 gives the MD5) and a configuration file that names every seed and design target, and the pipeline that built them is archived under its own DOI. A second build from the same configuration and the same source population, which is available on request (Section 5), reproduced all three files byte for byte.

3.2 Population characteristics

The simulated registry has the age and sex distribution of the cases reported to FCDS between 1995 and 2023 [1], which it was drawn to match by quota (Section 2); the agreement, within 0.041 percentage points in each of the 36 age and sex strata, is a check that the sampler hit its target rather than a finding about the population (Figure 1). 62% of registry records are people aged 65 or older at diagnosis and 4% are under 40; 48% are women. The finder files have the age structure of the simulated population’s Florida residents in 2040 instead: 26% of the larger file are 65 or older, 43% are under 40, and 51% are female.

By race and ethnicity, people in the registry are 64% White, 17% Latino, 12% Black, 5% Asian and 3% other or multiracial (American Indian and Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian and Pacific Islander, multiracial, and unknown), compared with 55%, 21%, 12%, 7% and 4% in the larger finder file; the difference follows from the registry’s older ages (Section 4). The two finder files differ from each other by at most 0.3 percentage points on every share reported in this section.

Registry records come from three censuses: 27% of them are from 2020, 28% from 2030 and 46% from 2040 (Section 3.1).

The three most common first names in each age group, printed at the ends of the bars in Figure 1, run from Liam, Noah, Oliver among boys under five to James, Robert, John among men of 85 and over, and from Olivia, Charlotte, Emma to Mary, Barbara, Patricia among girls and women.

Figure 2 shows three of the 100,000 people who appear in both the registry and the larger finder file, chosen to show three kinds of error, with every field that differs between their two records marked: a first name recorded as a nickname, an address altered in two fields with a wrong race/ethnicity category and a blank SSN, and a swapped month and day of birth beside a swapped pair of SSN digits. The two records of a pair are one census record noised twice, so every difference in the figure is an injected error and not a move or a change of name, a simplification weighed in Section 4.

3.3 Error structure

Table 2 gives the error structure field by field: the share of values that are blank in the registry and in the larger finder file, against the blanking rate set for each, and, among the 100,000 true pairs, the share of pairs whose two records agree exactly when both have a value and the share with a blank on either side. Agreeing exactly means the two values are the same string, character for character; the rules in Section 3.4 lower-case and trim values before comparing them (Section 2). The smaller finder file matches the larger on every figure in the table to within 0.8 percentage points.

SSNs are blank in 20.0% of finder records, the rate FCDS specified, and in 5.68% of registry records against a specified 5%. The build blanked no registry SSN, so every blank there is a person who never held one in the source population, where coverage varies with age: 3.8% of registry records for people under 40 at diagnosis lack an SSN against 6.4% for people of 40 to 64, and the registry’s ages are the ones with the least coverage, which is why its share sits above both the specification and the whole pool’s 4.18% (Section 2). Blank SSNs are also uneven by race/ethnicity: in the larger finder file 28.9% of Asian and 23.5% of Latino people’s records have none against 17.8% of White people’s, and in the registry the shares are 21.5%, 15.2% and 1.9%; Section 3.4 shows what this does to rules that depend on the SSN. Of the SSNs present in the larger finder file, 4,001 (1.0%) carry two adjacent digits swapped, and where a true pair has an SSN on both sides the two agree in 99.1% of pairs.

Names and dates of birth disagree more often than SSNs do. Among true pairs with both values present, first names agree in 94.0% of pairs, last names in 95.9% and dates of birth in 93.6%, and each of these fields is blank on one side in about 2.1% of pairs. Taken together, 79.3% of true pairs agree exactly on first name, last name and date of birth, and 77.9% have an SSN on both sides that agrees; these two shares bound what exact-match rules can find in Section 3.4. Address fields agree in 97.0% of pairs with both present and are blank on one side in 5.9%; the unit number is blank for 94% of registry records, because most addresses have none, and street numbers are blank above their set rates because some source addresses carry none.

The files also carry the patterns a user might check for as sentinels. Dates of birth are blank in 1.0% of registry records and 1.4% of those present do not parse as a calendar date, a month above twelve for example; 11 registry records carry a Doe-pattern name (John or Jane Doe); no SSN in any file is a single repeated digit; and 52 SSNs in the larger finder file, and none in the registry, fall in ranges the Social Security Administration does not issue.

3.4 Linkage difficulty

Exact keys are less unique than they look. Among the 5,000,000 people in the registry, 97.0% have a first name, last name and date of birth that no one else in the file shares, 88.8% have a unique last name and date of birth, and 81.6% a unique ZIP code, date of birth and sex, while 47% share their full name with at least one other person.

Table 3 scores exact-agreement rules on the larger finder file against the key. Agreement on first name, last name and date of birth links 79.3% of true pairs at a precision of 99.81%, and the SSN alone links 77.9% at 99.97%. The two field sets FCDS’s Procedure Guide requires a submission to carry [2] behave differently as exact rules: name, SSN and sex makes no false matches and finds 64.7% of true pairs, name with month and year of birth and sex admits 4,435 false matches, 5.5% of the pairs it proposes, and either set finds 81.5%; the two sets of FCDS’s current Data Linkage Record Layout [3], which both require the full date of birth, find 71.7% together with no false matches. Name and date of birth or SSN, the best simple rule, reaches a recall of 95.4% at a precision of 99.82%, and last name with date of birth alone falls to a precision of 71.0%. These are exact-agreement rules on the field sets FCDS requires a submission to carry, not the registry’s own matching procedure.

Without blocking the two files present 2.5 trillion record pairs. Blocking on the full date of birth leaves 58 million candidate pairs and keeps 91.7% of true pairs, the pairs whose dates of birth are present and agree on both sides (Table 2); blocking on the first letter of the last name with the year of birth leaves 1.23 billion and keeps 90.7%.

Figure 3 splits three rules by the race/ethnicity recorded on the finder record. For first name, last name and date of birth the missed-match rate is alike across groups, from 20.5% to 20.9%, and the false-match rate stays below 0.28% in every group. The SSN rule differs by group: it misses 34% of true pairs for Asian people and 29% for Latino people against 19% for White people, and the difference carries into the best simple rule, which misses 7.2% of Asian true pairs against 3.9% of White ones.

The 11 rules run in 3.8 seconds on the 500,000-record file with 8 threads on an eight-core allocation. The 100,000-record file gives the same picture: every rule’s recall is within 0.8 percentage points of the larger file’s.
